title: Χελιδὼν καὶ ὄρνιθες
part: The Swallow and the Birds (Chambry 349 · Perry 39)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 349 (= Perry 39). Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἄρτι τοῦ ἰξοῦ φυομένου, χελιδὼν αἰσθομένη τὸν ἐνιστάμενον τοῖς πετεινοῖς κίνδυνον, συναθροίσασα πάντα τὰ ὄρνεα, συνεβούλευσεν αὐτοῖς μάλιστα μὲν ταῖς ἰξοφόροις δρυσὶν ἐκκόψαι· εἰ δ’ ἄρα τοῦτο αὐτοῖς ἀδύνατον, ἐπὶ τοὺς ἀνθρώπους καταφυγεῖν καὶ τούτους ἱκετεῦσαι, ὅπως μὴ χρησάμενοι τῇ τοῦ ἰξοῦ ἐνεργείᾳ συλλαμβάνωσιν αὐτά.
sentences.tr: Arti tou ixou phyomenou, chelidōn aisthomenē ton enistamenon tois peteinois kindynon, synathroisasa panta ta ornea, synebouleusen autois malista men tais ixophorois drysin ekkopsai· ei d’ ara touto autois adynaton, epi tous anthrōpous kataphygein kai toutous hiketeusai, hopōs mē chrēsamenoi tēi tou ixou energeiāi syllambanōsin auta.
sentences.l: The mistletoe just now coming into growth, a swallow, perceiving the danger setting in for the winged creatures, having gathered together all the birds, advised them best of all to cut it away on the mistletoe-bearing oaks; but if that were impossible for them, to take refuge with men and to beseech them, so that they might not, using the power of the birdlime, catch them.
sentences.i: Just as the mistletoe was coming into growth, a swallow saw the danger hanging over the birds, gathered them all together, and advised them, best of all, to cut it away on the oaks that carried it; and, if that were beyond them, to take refuge with men and beg them not to use the force of birdlime to catch them.
sentences.n: ἰξός is the mistletoe, and also the birdlime boiled from its berries — one word for the plant and the glue, which is why the swallow's warning makes sense at the moment the plant appears. ἐνιστάμενον is the danger 'setting itself in the way', impending. μάλιστα μέν … εἰ δ’ ἄρα … is the standing pair, 'best of all … but if in fact …'. ὅπως μή with the subjunctive gives the content of the entreaty. One oddity, honestly: ἐκκόψαι is printed with the dative ταῖς ἰξοφόροις δρυσίν where an accusative, 'cut down the mistletoe-bearing oaks', would be expected; the dative reads most easily as the place, cutting the growth away on the trees that bear it, and the English follows that. The birds are called τὰ πετεινά, τὰ ὄρνεα and ὄρνιθες indifferently here; all are simply 'birds'.

sentences.t: Τῶν δὲ γελασάντων αὐτὴν ὡς ματαιολογοῦσαν, αὐτὴ παραγενομένη ἱκέτις τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐγένετο.
sentences.tr: Tōn de gelasantōn autēn hōs mataiologousan, autē paragenomenē hiketis tōn anthrōpōn egeneto.
sentences.l: And they having laughed at her as talking idly, she herself, having gone to them, became a suppliant of men.
sentences.i: They laughed at her for talking idly, so she went herself and became a suppliant of men.
sentences.n: γελάω takes the accusative of the person laughed at. ὡς with the participle gives the birds' own view of the matter, not the fable's: they laughed at her for, as they saw it, talking nonsense. αὐτή with the smooth breathing is 'she herself', to be kept apart from αὕτη, 'this one'.

sentences.t: Οἱ δὲ ἀποδεξάμενοι αὐτὴν ἐπὶ τῇ συνέσει καὶ σύνοικον αὐτὴν προσελάβοντο.
sentences.tr: Hoi de apodexamenoi autēn epi tēi synesei kai synoikon autēn proselabonto.
sentences.l: And they, having welcomed her for her understanding, took her to themselves as a housemate as well.
sentences.i: They welcomed her for her good sense, and took her in besides to live under their own roof.
sentences.n: ἐπί with the dative gives the ground of the welcome — received for her good sense. προσελάβοντο is middle: they took her to their own side, and so into their own houses. καί is 'as well': first the welcome, then the further step of sharing a roof.

sentences.t: Οὕτως συνέβη τὰ μὲν λοιπὰ ἀγρευόμενα ὑπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων κατεσθίεσθαι, μόνην δὲ τὴν χελιδόνα ὡς πρόσφυγα καὶ ἐν ταῖς αὐτῶν οἰκίαις ἀδεῶς νεοττοποιεῖσθαι.
sentences.tr: Houtōs synebē ta men loipa agreuomena hypo tōn anthrōpōn katesthiesthai, monēn de tēn chelidona hōs prosphyga kai en tais autōn oikiais adeōs neottopoieisthai.
sentences.l: So it came about that the rest, being hunted by men, are eaten up, but that the swallow alone, as one fled to them for refuge, builds her nest even in their houses without fear.
sentences.i: So it came about that all the other birds are hunted by men and eaten, while the swallow alone, having put herself under their protection, nests unafraid even inside their houses.
sentences.n: συνέβη carries two accusative-and-infinitive clauses, μέν against δέ. πρόσφυξ is one who has fled to another for shelter — the same standing as the ἱκέτις above, and the reason the swallow lives indoors. αὐτῶν, 'their', is the men's.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι οἱ τὰ μέλλοντα προορώμενοι εἰκότως τοὺς κινδύνους διακρούονται.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti hoi ta mellonta proorōmenoi eikotōs tous kindynous diakrouontai.
sentences.l: The story shows that those who foresee the things to come naturally beat off dangers.
sentences.n: τὰ μέλλοντα is the participle of μέλλω used as a noun, 'the things about to be'. διακρούομαι in the middle is to knock a thing aside from oneself, to fend it off. εἰκότως is 'as is to be expected' — the escape follows from the foresight, not from luck.
